CausalChain: HCC cells under hypoxia -> HIF-1α upregulates ENTPD2 -> ENTPD2 converts extracellular ATP to 5′ AMP -> Increased 5′ AMP promotes recruitment/activation of MDSCs -> MDSCs suppress T cell function and enhance immunosuppression -> Reduced T cell antitumor activity leads to poor response to ICIs -> Inhibition of ENTPD2 would diminish MDSC accumulation -> Restored T cell function enhances ICI efficacy in HCC
Hypothesis: In hepatocellular carcinoma, targeting ENTPD2 to block the ATP-to-5′ AMP conversion will reduce myeloid-derived suppressor cell recruitment, thereby relieving immunosuppression and enhancing the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade therapy.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is notoriously resistant to immune checkpoint blockade in part due to the highly immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment. Emerging evidence indicates that under hypoxic conditions, HCC cells upregulate molecules such as ENTPD2 via HIF‐1α signaling. ENTPD2 converts extracellular ATP into 5′ AMP, a metabolite implicated in the recruitment and activation of myeloid‐derived suppressor cells (MDSCs). MDSCs foster an immunosuppressive milieu by inhibiting cytotoxic T lymphocytes and enhancing regulatory cell populations. Here, we propose that pharmacologic inhibition or genetic downregulation of ENTPD2 in HCC may reduce MDSC accumulation and function, thereby restoring effective T cell–mediated antitumor immunity and synergizing with immune checkpoint inhibitors. This hypothesis provides a mechanistic framework to explore a novel therapeutic target in HCC immune modulation.
